Retrospective study

READING STUDIES

Retrospective study

Also found as: retrospective · retrospective chart review

In plain language

A study that looks back at events or treatment that have already occurred. The knee-pain paper describes a retrospective chart review followed by patient contact.[1]

Source check: 2026-10-04 · Editorial method

On this page
How the research uses this term
Reading the evidence
Used in our guides
Related terms
References
Browse all 54 terms
How the research uses this term

The researchers identified patients who had received injections and asked about their knee pain afterward. Follow-up timing varied between patients.[1]

The knee report assembled records from an existing clinical practice after injections had already been given, so the research began with previously treated patients rather than a newly assigned trial population.[1]

The authors excluded a person who could not be reached for follow-up, which makes the reported observations dependent on the patients whose later accounts were available to the investigators.[1]

Follow-up callers asked patients to rate their pain before and after treatment and to describe mobility, exercise tolerance, stair climbing and sleep, rather than collecting a uniform set of objective performance tests.[1]

The report describes using a peptide combination initially and later trying BPC157 alone, a clinical sequence that differs from randomly assigning comparable patients to concurrent treatment groups.[1]

Reading the evidence

This design differs from assigning treatment prospectively and following a predefined control group. The paper's symptom reports do not isolate treatment effects from all other possible reasons for change.[1]

Patients did not all have the same underlying knee condition, and the discussion acknowledges that diagnoses were not established with the same imaging and other investigations for every participant.[1]

The abstract states that no specific tools measured function, quality of life, stiffness or activities of daily living, identifying outcome gaps that remain despite the availability of later patient accounts.[1]

A request for future imaging and treatment comparisons is a research recommendation within this paper, rather than evidence that the observed symptom changes already demonstrate structural repair or a treatment advantage.[1]

Time to peak concentration (Tmax)

DRUG BEHAVIOR & DELIVERY

Time to peak concentration (Tmax)

Also found as: Tmax · time to peak concentration

In plain language

The time at which a drug's plasma concentration reaches its peak. This is the meaning given to Tmax in the BPC-157 pharmacokinetic tables.[1]

Source check: 2026-10-04 · Editorial method

On this page
How the research uses this term
Reading the evidence
Related terms
References
Browse all 54 terms
How the research uses this term

The paper reports Tmax for the studied intramuscular administrations alongside Cmax and AUC. It locates the concentration peak within the sampling period.[1]

The rat and dog tables place the timing of the concentration peak alongside the size of that peak and the exposure accumulated over time, keeping these pharmacokinetic descriptions as separate quantities.[1]

The study presents separate tables for intravenous and intramuscular administration and for different animal species, so the meaning of a reported peak time remains attached to the route and experimental group.[1]

Blood was collected at scheduled times after administration and the plasma was analyzed for BPC157, making the timing estimate part of a sampled concentration profile rather than continuous observation inside the animal.[1]

The investigators also sampled animals during repeated administration experiments, which should be distinguished from the profiles obtained after an initial administration when interpreting a table or plotted concentration curve.[1]

Reading the evidence

This is the time to a concentration peak, not the time to clinical improvement. The experiment measured drug exposure and disposition in rats and dogs.[1]

The radioactive tracer experiment reports a peak for total radioactivity as well as the separate parent-drug experiments, so a peak in labeled material should not automatically be identified as a peak of unchanged BPC157.[1]

The paper distinguishes parent-drug concentration from radioactive material that can include breakdown products, an analytical distinction that matters before comparing the timing of peaks across its different experiments.[1]

These peak-time observations describe the disposition of the experimental preparations in rats and dogs, and the study does not measure the time at which an injured human tendon or joint improves.[1]

Home

Glossary
/
Histology

READING STUDIES

Histology

Also found as: histological · histopathological · histopathology

In plain language

The microscopic study of tissue structure. In the rat Achilles paper, histological evaluation examines stained sections of healing tendons.[1]

Source check: 2026-10-04 · Editorial method

On this page
How the research uses this term
Reading the evidence
Related terms
References
Browse all 54 terms
How the research uses this term

The authors used staining and scoring methods to assess features of the repaired tissue. They also assessed collagen expression with immunohistochemical methods.[1]

The tendon study examines an experimentally ruptured and surgically repaired Achilles tendon in rats, giving the tissue images a defined injury model rather than treating them as observations of untreated human tendon disease.[1]

Tendons assigned to microscopy were processed separately from those assigned to mechanical testing, so the stained sections and the measured breaking loads do not represent repeated measurements on the same specimen.[1]

Longitudinal sections allowed assessment of fiber architecture, cell shape and collagen organization across the repair region, while different stains emphasized different features of the tissue being examined.[1]

The scoring systems considered characteristics such as collagen arrangement, cellular appearance, vascularity and ground substance, making a histological score a summary of specified tissue features rather than an unrestricted measure of recovery.[1]

Reading the evidence

The same paper measured load to failure separately. Its microscopic and mechanical assessments used different tendon samples, so a histological score should not be relabeled as a measurement of tendon strength.[1]

The authors caution that differences seen with polarized staining may reflect collagen fiber alignment and organization rather than greater collagen production, preserving the distinction between tissue appearance and a claim about synthesis.[1]

A pathologist assessed coded tissue without knowing its treatment assignment, but the paper also states that surgery and daily treatment could not be blinded and that agreement between multiple observers was not assessed.[1]

The authors identify the assessment period, healthy young rat model and absence of functional testing as limits, so microscopic organization at that stage does not establish later maturation or recovery of human activity.[1]

Home
/
Glossary
/
Area under the curve (AUC)

DRUG BEHAVIOR & DELIVERY

Area under the curve (AUC)

Also found as: AUC · area under the curve · area under the concentration-time curve

In plain language

A summary of concentration across a span of time. In the BPC-157 paper, AUC is the area beneath the plasma concentration-versus-time curve.[1]

Source check: 2026-10-04 · Editorial method

On this page
How the research uses this term
Reading the evidence
Related terms
References
Browse all 54 terms
How the research uses this term

The paper distinguishes AUC up to the last observation from AUC extrapolated to infinity. These refer to different time limits for the exposure estimate.[1]

The exposure tables distinguish the area accumulated through the final observation from an area extrapolated beyond the observed samples, making the stated time boundary part of the interpretation of an AUC value.[1]

The same exposure summary is reported in separate rat and dog experiments and after different administration routes, so the species, route and sampling design belong with the reported estimate.[1]

The authors use dose-adjusted exposure after intramuscular administration and an intravenous reference to estimate bioavailability, illustrating a specific comparison rather than making an AUC value itself a percentage absorbed.[1]

The tables report peak concentration beside accumulated exposure because a concentration maximum and the area across a concentration profile describe different aspects of the measurements collected in the experiment.[1]

Reading the evidence

AUC and Cmax answer different questions: the first summarizes exposure across time, while the second identifies the peak concentration. Both appear in the study's pharmacokinetic tables.[1]

The study examines how exposure relates to the administered amount within its tested animal experiments and also describes repeated administration separately, without turning those relationships into a clinical treatment schedule.[1]

Exposure calculated from total radioactivity includes labeled material remaining after peptide breakdown, and the paper separates that signal from the plasma profile of unchanged parent BPC157.[1]

The study did not analyze metabolites within the target tissues, so its exposure summaries cannot identify how much unchanged peptide reached an injured human tendon or establish a healing effect there.[1]

Glossary
/
Absorption

DRUG BEHAVIOR & DELIVERY

Absorption

Also found as: absorbed

In plain language

The process by which material from an administered preparation enters the body. The collagen trial examines the appearance of amino acids in blood after ingestion.[1]

Source check: 2026-10-04 · Editorial method

On this page
How the research uses this term
Reading the evidence
Used in our guides
Related terms
References
Browse all 54 terms
How the research uses this term

Researchers took blood samples before and after participants consumed different collagen preparations. They compared the resulting amino-acid concentration profiles.[1]

The collagen experiment studied healthy men in an acute crossover design, with the same participants attending separate experimental visits rather than following patients through a course of treatment for an injury.[1]

Participants consumed an enzymatically hydrolyzed collagen product, a non-enzymatically hydrolyzed product and a water placebo on separate visits, allowing the investigators to compare the subsequent blood profiles under the study conditions.[1]

The protocol standardized preparation for the visits and collected blood before and after beverage consumption, linking the absorption observations to those particular products and the controlled experimental setting.[1]

The laboratory analysis quantified amino acids in plasma, so the measured appearance of collagen components in the circulation is distinct from detecting an entire ingested collagen protein or proving that it entered damaged tissue.[1]

Reading the evidence

In that trial, the measured substances were circulating amino acids. This does not mean that the entire ingested collagen protein entered the blood unchanged.[1]

The investigators reported a different absorption pattern for glycine, proline and hydroxyproline after enzymatic processing, but did not find the same processing advantage across all of the amino acids they examined.[1]

Total amino acids, essential amino acids and branched chain amino acids did not distinguish the collagen products in the same way as those particular abundant collagen components, limiting a broad claim that processing improved every absorption measure.[1]

The study discusses possible tissue implications in relation to other research, while its own experiment measures the post-meal blood response rather than directly demonstrating tendon healing, cartilage regeneration or relief of joint pain.[1]

Fibroblast

MECHANISMS & HORMONES

Fibroblast

Also found as: fibroblasts · tendon fibroblasts

In plain language

A connective-tissue cell involved in producing extracellular matrix. The tendon paper describes fibroblasts making collagen and other matrix components during repair.[1]

Source check: 2026-10-04 · Editorial method

On this page
How the research uses this term
Reading the evidence
Used in our guides
Related terms
References
Browse all 54 terms
How the research uses this term

The experiment isolated tendon fibroblasts from rats, cultured them and studied their responses to BPC-157 and growth hormone. Receptor expression, proliferation and signaling were measured separately.[1]

The investigators obtained Achilles tendon tissue from rats and grew cells from the tissue fragments in culture, so the fibroblasts in this experiment were studied outside an intact injured animal or human participant.[1]

The cultured cells were maintained in laboratory medium and exposed to BPC157 under specified incubation conditions, an experimental preparation that differs from measuring what reaches a tendon after administration to a person.[1]

Control cultures and BPC157-treated cultures were examined at defined stages of incubation, allowing the authors to investigate cellular changes within that culture system rather than treating a clinical symptom report as a cell measurement.[1]

The paper describes a receptor-expression clue from earlier screening work and then examines growth hormone receptor RNA and protein in the current experiments, distinguishing a proposed cellular explanation from direct evidence of tissue healing.[1]

Reading the evidence

Cell proliferation means the cells are increasing in number. In this study, that cellular readout is not a direct test of the mechanical strength of a healed tendon.[1]

The authors assessed viable cells with a laboratory assay and also examined a proliferation-associated marker, keeping these cellular readouts separate from a mechanical test of whether a repaired tendon can withstand loading.[1]

Growth hormone was added after BPC157 pretreatment in the response experiments, so the observed cell behavior relates to that sequence of exposures rather than showing that BPC157 itself is growth hormone.[1]

The authors identify the in vitro design as a limitation and call for further work to connect the cellular findings with tendon healing, leaving clinical effectiveness and an appropriate human treatment regimen unestablished by these cultures.[1]

Home

Glossary
/
Peak concentration (Cmax)

DRUG BEHAVIOR & DELIVERY

Peak concentration (Cmax)

Also found as: Cmax · peak concentration · maximum concentration

In plain language

The peak measured concentration of a drug in plasma. The BPC-157 paper labels this quantity Cmax.[1]

Source check: 2026-10-04 · Editorial method

On this page
How the research uses this term
Reading the evidence
Related terms
References
Browse all 54 terms
How the research uses this term

After administration, the researchers sampled plasma over time and reported the peak concentration alongside the time at which it occurred, Tmax.[1]

The peak is reported together with the time at which it occurs and the area accumulated across the profile, allowing readers to distinguish the height, timing and overall extent of exposure in the animal experiment.[1]

The rat and dog results are organized separately and include different experimental administrations, so a peak concentration should be read with the species and route that produced the sampled plasma profile.[1]

The parent peptide was quantified in plasma using a mass spectrometry method after scheduled blood sampling, tying the reported peak to a specified analyte and the measurements obtained in that experiment.[1]

The investigators examined both initial and repeated administration profiles, which means that a peak reported for a repeated exposure should not silently be substituted for one from an initial exposure.[1]

Reading the evidence

Cmax is a concentration measurement. The BPC-157 experiment used it to characterize drug exposure in animals, rather than as a direct measurement of wound healing.[1]

A maximum based on total radioactivity in the tracer experiment describes labeled material rather than only unchanged BPC157, and the paper explicitly compares those tracer results with its parent-drug measurements.[1]

The analysis of breakdown products and the lack of metabolite measurements within target tissues limit what a circulating peak can reveal about the identity of material present at a proposed site of action.[1]

The experiment characterizes drug disposition in animals and does not pair a particular plasma peak with a measured improvement in human wound healing, pain or physical function.[1]

Home
/
Glossary
/
Receptor

MECHANISMS & HORMONES

Receptor

Also found as: receptors

In plain language

A molecular target through which a signal can act on a cell. The tendon-cell paper describes growth hormone binding to its receptor on the cell membrane and activating intracellular signaling.[1]

Source check: 2026-10-04 · Editorial method

On this page
How the research uses this term
Reading the evidence
Used in our guides
Related terms
References
Browse all 54 terms
How the research uses this term

The investigators separately measured receptor expression and the response to added growth hormone. They assessed receptor RNA and protein as well as cell proliferation and JAK2 pathway activation.[1]

The tendon-cell experiment assessed growth hormone receptor RNA and protein with different laboratory methods, so an expression result identifies a change in the measured receptor material rather than a measurement of circulating growth hormone.[1]

The investigators exposed cultured rat tendon fibroblasts to BPC157 before assessing receptor expression, retaining the cell type and experimental preparation as part of what the reported response describes.[1]

In the response experiments, growth hormone was added to cells that had already received BPC157 pretreatment, separating the preparation associated with altered expression from the hormone used to test the subsequent response.[1]

The authors examined downstream signaling after hormone addition as well as receptor expression, which distinguishes the amount of a measured receptor from a separate observation about the signaling pathway it can engage.[1]

Reading the evidence

More receptor expression and a downstream cellular response are distinct observations. In this paper they come from cultured rat tendon cells; they are not direct measurements of injury healing in human participants.[1]

The signaling analysis distinguished activated pathway protein from the total amount of that protein, illustrating why a change in activation should not be relabeled as an increase in every component of the pathway.[1]

These observations came from cells maintained in culture and analyzed after controlled exposures, rather than receptor measurements from a human tendon during a randomized clinical trial of injury treatment.[1]

The paper treats the cellular findings as a possible explanation requiring further investigation, so receptor expression and signaling do not by themselves establish that a preparation improves tendon strength or clinical recovery.[1]

Home

Glossary
/
Patient-reported outcome

READING STUDIES

Patient-reported outcome

Also found as: patient-reported · patient reported · subjective symptoms

In plain language

An outcome reported by the participant, such as their experience of pain. The knee study asked treated patients about their knee symptoms.[1]

Source check: 2026-10-04 · Editorial method

On this page
How the research uses this term
Reading the evidence
Used in our guides
Related terms
References
Browse all 54 terms
How the research uses this term

The authors collected retrospective reports of symptom change. They stated that no specific tools were used to assess function, quality of life, stiffness or activities of daily living.[1]

The knee study obtained later accounts through telephone follow-up conducted by a volunteer, so the symptom descriptions came from patients recalling their experience rather than from an observer examining the joint at that visit.[1]

Patients were asked to describe pain before and after the injection as well as mobility, tolerance for exercise, stair climbing and sleep, giving the report several different kinds of perceived change.[1]

The callers also asked about adverse events and allowed patients to comment on their treatment, collecting personal accounts without turning those accounts into a systematic laboratory assessment of safety.[1]

The authors explicitly state that the measurements were subjective and that no objective testing verified the reported improvements, keeping the patients' experiences distinct from a directly measured physical performance outcome.[1]

Reading the evidence

These reports describe patients' experiences. The paper calls for future imaging, so reported pain relief should not be rewritten as an imaging-confirmed finding of structural healing.[1]

Follow-up timing varied and a patient who could not be reached was excluded, so the available accounts do not represent a uniform observation period or information from every person initially identified.[1]

Imaging was available for some patients before treatment, but the paper calls for future investigations of structural change rather than presenting serial imaging as confirmation of the reported symptom improvements.[1]

The observations arose from an uncontrolled retrospective practice report involving different knee problems, so subjective improvement does not by itself establish how treatment compares with another intervention or with the course without treatment.[1]

Home
/
Glossary
/
Biomechanical testing

READING STUDIES

Biomechanical testing

Also found as: biomechanical · biomechanics · maximum load to failure · load to failure

In plain language

Testing a biological tissue's mechanical behavior. The Achilles repair paper measures the maximum load a repaired rat tendon withstands before failure.[1]

Source check: 2026-10-04 · Editorial method

On this page
How the research uses this term
Reading the evidence
Used in our guides
Related terms
References
Browse all 54 terms
How the research uses this term

This endpoint is different from looking at tissue under a microscope. The study used mechanical testing and histological evaluation as separate assessments of the repaired tendons.[1]

The investigators tested excised Achilles tendon specimens with their attachments using a tensile testing device, recording the greatest load reached before failure within that laboratory arrangement rather than measuring pain during walking.[1]

Specimens allocated to mechanical testing were stored before assessment and coded for blinded testing, while a different set of tendons was processed for microscopy and tissue staining.[1]

The tested tendons came from a standardized rat rupture and surgical repair model, which defines the injury and repair conditions associated with the observed loads and limits direct comparison with other injury models.[1]

The study did not find a significant increase in maximum load to failure for BPC157 compared with controls despite some histological changes, illustrating why microscopic observations should not be substituted for a mechanical endpoint.[1]

Reading the evidence

The experimental model involved surgically injured and repaired rat Achilles tendons. The measured load describes those specimens, rather than a patient's pain, mobility or return to sport.[1]

The authors did not measure tendon cross-sectional area, which prevented calculation of stress-based mechanical properties and limits what the reported load alone says about the material properties of the repaired tissue.[1]

The paper also identifies missing stiffness, energy-to-failure and failure-mode analyses, so the reported maximum load does not cover every aspect of how a tendon behaves under mechanical loading.[1]

Functional activity was not assessed and the work used healthy young rats at a defined repair stage, leaving return to human sport, later maturation and performance in patients with other illnesses outside these measurements.[1]
